title: The day Duren burned
pull: A town erased in half an hour

facts.text: Before the war about 45,000 people lived in Duren, a prosperous factory town on the Roer River between Aachen and Cologne. By late 1944, with the front only a few miles away, about 22,000 were still living in its roughly 10,000 houses.

On 16 November 1944, a sunny Thursday afternoon, nearly 500 British bombers flew toward Duren. From about 3:25 p.m., in less than half an hour, they dropped explosive and incendiary bombs on the town.

The raid was part of Operation Queen, the Allied offensive toward the Roer. RAF Bomber Command was given the task of destroying Duren, Julich and Heinsberg to block the roads German reinforcements would use.
The Australian War Memorial records 485 Lancasters and 13 Mosquitos on Duren. German local history counts 474 bombers and 2,751 tons of bombs.
Between 3,106 and 3,127 people were killed in Duren that day, most of them civilians, by the counts of the Australian War Memorial and German local historians.

Forced laborers working in armaments factories died in disproportionate numbers, because they were often not allowed into shelters. After the raids they were made to clear the rubble and the unexploded bombs.
Duren was 99 percent destroyed, the most heavily destroyed town in Germany by local reckoning. Julich, bombed the same afternoon, was 97 percent destroyed.
German soldiers were in the towns too. Signal and headquarters troops were hit in Duren, and an artillery battalion arriving by train was all but wiped out at the Julich station.
Duren was bombed 51 times in all before the war ended. American troops took the ruins in February 1945.
Both towns still mark the day every 16 November. In Julich, a wreath is laid at the memorial at 3:25 p.m.

NARA 111-SC-293168 (naId 404791009), use Unrestricted, public domain. NARA production date is July 1945; the photo was taken after the town's capture in late February 1945, so it shows the ruins about three months after the raid, not the raid day. Cropped off the print border, 1920 x 1524, grayscale. Frame on the road and the ruined house at right. photoCredit: The main street of Duren, Germany, in ruins, 1945. US Army Signal Corps photo, NARA 111-SC-293168, public domain.

declassified.fact: By June 1945 only 3,806 people were left living in Duren. The Allies first discussed rebuilding the town on a new site south of the rubble mountains, but the people of Duren insisted on rebuilding where it had always stood, and by the end of 1945 returning residents and refugees had pushed the population back above 25,000.

body:
In less than half an hour on a sunny Thursday afternoon, a town of 22,000 people was almost wiped off the map.

16 November 1944. From about 3:25 p.m., nearly 500 British bombers dropped explosive and incendiary bombs on Duren, a factory town on the Roer River between Aachen and Cologne. RAF Bomber Command had been told to destroy it, with Julich and Heinsberg, to block the roads German reinforcements would use.

Between 3,106 and 3,127 people were killed, most of them civilians. Forced laborers in the armaments factories died in disproportionate numbers, because they were often kept out of the shelters.

Duren was 99 percent destroyed. Every 16 November, Julich still lays a wreath at 3:25 p.m.
